passage_text: Researchers studied the effect of a new antihypertensive drug on systolic blood pressure (SBP) in 390 adults with stage‑1 hypertension. Participants were enrolled from three community clinics and followed for 12 weeks. Baseline SBP was measured after a 5‑minute seated rest, and the drug was administered once daily at 8:00 a.m. Blood pressure readings were taken at baseline and at 12 weeks by the same trained technician using a calibrated oscillometric cuff. The study was designed as a single‑group, pre‑post intervention without a control arm. Demographic data were collected, and participants were stratified into three age groups: 40–50, 51–60, and 61–70 years. The investigators reported mean SBP reductions for each group and performed paired t‑tests to assess statistical significance. No serious adverse events were reported, and the drug was well tolerated. The authors concluded that the medication effectively lowered SBP across all age strata, with the greatest absolute reduction observed in the oldest cohort.
stem: Which age group showed the greatest reduction in mean systolic blood pressure?

options.D: All three groups had the same reduction

explanation: Correct: reductions were 5 (40-50), 12 (51-60) and 15 mmHg (61-70). Why the others are wrong: A) Reduction was only 5 mmHg. B) Reduction was 12 mmHg, smaller than 15. D) Reductions were 5, 12 and 15 mmHg.
trap: Judging by the similar post-treatment means (135, 133, 135 mmHg) and concluding the effect was equal, instead of subtracting each post value from its baseline.

stem: Which of the following best describes the study design used by the researchers?
explanation: Correct: one group received the drug and was measured before and after, with no control arm. Why the others are wrong: A) There was no randomization and no control arm. C) Participants were not selected by outcome status and compared for past exposure. D) SBP was measured twice over 12 weeks, not at one time point.
trap: Seeing an intervention and assuming a randomized trial.

stem: What is the percent reduction in mean SBP for the 61‑70 age group?
explanation: Percent reduction = (150 – 135)/150 × 100 = 15/150 × 100 = 10%. The closest option is 10%.
trap: Reading the 15 mmHg absolute reduction as 15% (option C) without dividing by the 150 mmHg baseline.

stem: Which design feature most limits the conclusion that the drug caused the SBP reductions?

options.A: The absence of a control group
options.B: Use of a calibrated oscillometric cuff
options.C: Having the same trained technician take all readings
options.D: Stratifying participants into three age groups

explanation: Correct: without a control group, changes could be due to time, regression to the mean or expectation rather than the drug. Why the others are wrong: B) A calibrated cuff reduces measurement error. C) A single technician reduces variability between observers. D) Stratification describes subgroups and does not weaken causal inference.
trap: Treating measurement-standardization steps as the main limitation.

stem: Which statement best links the study findings to clinical practice?

options.A: The drug is effective in all age groups, so it should replace all current antihypertensives.
options.B: The drug should not be used in patients younger than 60 years.
options.C: Mean SBP fell in all three age groups, most in the 61–70 group, but without a control arm the drug’s causal effect is not established.
options.D: The drug increases SBP and is contraindicated.

explanation: Correct: Reductions were 5, 12 and 15 mmHg; the study had no control arm, so causation and comparison with other drugs cannot be concluded. Why the others are wrong: A) No other antihypertensive was compared, and there was no control arm. B) Younger groups also had a fall in SBP (5 and 12 mmHg). D) SBP fell in every group.
trap: Reading a before-and-after fall in a single group as proof that the drug works better than, or should replace, existing treatment.
